column3: Repeats the settlement elites' refusal of the message brought by a warner.
Pairs a truth-bearing descent with the messenger's warning office.
Contrasts the inherited path with a detailed book given as guidance and mercy.
States outright disbelief in the message others have accepted.
The immediately preceding question exposes the absence of a held scriptural warrant.
Shows disbelievers calling a presented sign and its bearers false.
Directly repeats rejection of what multiple messengers were sent with.
Supplies the immediate ancestral-imitation premise answered in the focus ayah.
A claimed readiness for better guidance is tested by clear guidance actually arriving.
Defines ancestral following itself as supposedly sufficient guidance.
Invokes the prior messenger tradition against unauthorized inherited worship.
Gives following a trustworthy, rightly guided messenger as the alternative criterion.
Directly rejects ancestral imitation when the ancestors neither reason nor receive guidance.
Generalizes the recurring role of a warner entering a settlement.
Condemns the human disposition toward covering received truth.
Directly opposes returning to revelation and the messenger with ancestral sufficiency.
Provides the immediate consequence for the falsifiers described in the focus context.
Shares the language of bringing a grave claim, without the guidance comparison.
Frames a messenger's challenge to reconsider even when a clear proof is brought.
Locates ancestral indulgence before the arrival of truth and a clear messenger.
The disbelievers' reaction to the summons on the Last Day does not illuminate inherited guidance.
Directly portrays ancestral following maintained even when it leads to punishment.
Within the surah, divine guidance is asserted rather than inferred from inheritance.
Its scene of witnesses on judgment does not address testing an inherited path.
Messengers bring clear proofs, yet their hearers explicitly reject what they were sent with.
Restates the messenger's paired function of good news and warning.
The warning against despair is unrelated to evaluating a messenger's guidance.
Shows truth met with conditional demands and a repeated, collective refusal.
Within the surah, Moses is sent with signs and openly identifies his commission.
The accusation against Mary has no material relation to ancestral imitation or guidance.
An inherited practice is falsely attributed to God and corrected by revealed truth.
Noah's warning call is only a general messenger parallel.
The verse concerns corrupt ritual practice and punishment, not the focus's comparison of guidance.
A messenger brings truth and a clear proof for his people to assess.
Within the surah, it establishes the repeated sending of prophets among earlier peoples.
Connects bringing truth with affirming it rather than dismissing it in advance.
Exposes selective belief that rejects confirming truth outside an inherited possession.
Defines the messenger as a clear warner, matching the focus's incoming challenge.
Shows disbelievers gathering before the messenger without specifying their inherited rationale.
Jesus brings clear proofs and wisdom to clarify disputed matters and call for obedience.
Its exemplary history is nearby surah context but adds no guidance-comparison route.
Names persistent disbelief without the focus's ancestral or evidentiary structure.
The final confirmation of promises does not address reception of a better path.
Opposition to God and the messenger follows the descent of clear signs.
Moses brings clear proofs, while powerful hearers respond with arrogance.
Mentions fathers in a different ritual comparison rather than inherited religious authority.
The surah's wealth-and-disbelief context only secondarily recalls elite resistance.
Clear proofs are followed by an idolatrous turn rather than responsive guidance.
Limits loyalty to fathers when they prefer disbelief over faith.
Names revelation's descent but does not address its rejection or comparison with tradition.
The messengers say they have brought the matter their hearers had doubted.
Challenges an unreasoned religious assumption, but not an inherited path specifically.
Within the surah, a claimed turn to guidance is made under pressure rather than conviction.
Affirms that divine guidance cannot be displaced, without the focus's reception scene.
A messenger presents concrete signs from his Lord for his people to evaluate.
Fear of the unseen and the Hour is not a route to the focus's ancestral-guidance dispute.
The penitent heart's arrival at judgment is unrelated to refusing a messenger's better guidance.
Joseph abandons a disbelieving ancestral religion, offering only a secondary inverse parallel.
The closing command to turn away peacefully does not develop the focus's comparison.
Calls all people to follow the messenger so that they may be guided.
Forgetting a revealed share leads to division, but no inherited-path comparison is made.
States ancestral worship as the sole rationale that the prophet proceeds to challenge.
Records disbelief after the wished-for reminder is actually received.
The dietary ruling has no material connection to the focus.
The surah's account of worldly ranks and divine mercy only indirectly frames elite resistance.
Defines the security of those whose faith remains free of wrongdoing.
The parable of invalidated charity does not concern inherited guidance or messenger rejection.
Limits knowledge to God while defining the speaker as a clear warner.
Abraham's sound heart does not address the focus's reception of better guidance.
The declaration that none can protect from God is unrelated to ancestral imitation.
The dialogue of the condemned in the Hereafter does not illuminate the focus's reception scene.
Its demand for evidence offers a distant parallel to refusing unsupported claims.
Directly grounds guidance in divine responsibility rather than inherited custom.
A warner's threat establishes the consequence of refusing the warning.
Links disbelief with actively blocking God's path.
The messenger confirms that he delivered his Lord's messages and gave counsel to rejecters.
The immediate surah context exposes a baseless claim about worship as mere conjecture.
Disbelief in God and His messenger explains rejected acts, but lacks the focus's comparison.
Directly depicts a messenger accused of turning people from their fathers' way and refused belief.
Truthful witness and knowledge are nearby surah themes but not the focus's reception dispute.
Denial of God's signs is directly opposed to receiving divine guidance.
The immediate context calls arriving truth magic and expressly rejects it.
Describes the fate of a stubborn denier without the focus's guidance structure.
Begins the inquiry that challenges a people's inherited attachment to idols.
Contrasts outward messenger testimony with inward falsehood, only indirectly related to reception.
Explicitly judges both the people and their fathers to be in manifest error.
Moses explicitly offers to guide Pharaoh toward his Lord.
The people defend their practice solely by having found their fathers doing it.
Messengers bring an announcement to Abraham, but not a guidance-comparison scene.
A near warning culminates in the denier's regret, showing the cost of refusal.
Questions ancestral resurrection, touching ancestry but not inherited religious guidance.
Names the revelation as guidance and contrasts it with denial of God's signs.
Mutual waiting between opponents does not illuminate the focus.
Classifies persistent rejection as genuine disbelief and associates it with humiliation.
Shows a call to faith dismissed by disparaging those who have already believed.
States the prepared consequence for disbelievers, without the focus's causal detail.
Notes the continuity of earlier messengers but offers no reception-of-guidance parallel.
Divine guidance opens a path while leaving gratitude or denial as the human response.
The raising of dust has no material relation to the focus.
Mentions one who was denied, but does not develop inherited following or better guidance.
The people reject Hud's call because it would require abandoning what their fathers worshipped.
Salih's people resist the command to leave the worship inherited from their fathers.
Shuayb's people treat ancestral worship as the practice his call would prohibit.
Rejecters accuse the messengers of seeking to turn them from what their fathers worshipped.
Elites dismiss a messenger while appealing to a practice never found among their forefathers.
Directly invites a book from God that is more guiding than the available alternatives.
States the feared cost of following guidance that has arrived with the messenger.
Explains the followers' error by their finding their fathers already astray.
Abraham opens his challenge by asking what his father and people worship.
Abraham dissociates himself from the worship inherited from his father and people.
Commands holding fast to revelation and identifies it as a straight path.
Begins Abraham's confrontation with his father's idolatrous inherited practice.
Rejects deity-names invented by the hearers and their fathers without divine authority.
Abraham directly questions his father's inherited worship of what cannot hear or help.
Abraham asks his father and people what object they worship before exposing its failure.
Denies authority for names devised by the hearers and their fathers.
A confirming book arrives, yet those who had expected it disbelieve when it comes.
A messenger confirming prior scripture is met by a party that throws scripture aside.
Calls recipients of scripture to believe in the confirming revelation before consequence follows.
A messenger arrives to clarify what was concealed from scripture and to pardon much.
A messenger comes after an interval to remove the excuse that no warner arrived.
Every sign from the Lord is met by turning away.
Hearers listen to the messenger while their hearts remain veiled from understanding it.
The deniers reject not the messenger personally but God's signs.
Treats denial of God's signs as the cause of punishment.
Sets the recurring messenger pattern and the required response of piety and reform.
Contrasts that response with denying signs and arrogantly refusing them.
Reports that prior peoples received clear proofs yet would not believe after earlier denial.
Commands following the unlettered messenger and associates that following with guidance.
The deniers demand that the recited revelation be changed or replaced rather than received.
Shows people denying a message before comprehending it or seeing its interpretation.
Recounts messengers bringing clear proofs to peoples entrenched in prior denial.
Noah challenges his people to consider a clear proof and mercy they dislike.
Names the revealed truth while observing that most people do not believe.
Explains that every messenger speaks in the people's language so the message may be made clear.
Establishes the universal messenger call to worship God and avoid false objects of worship.
Records the objection that a human messenger cannot be believed.
Defines messengers as bearers of good news and warning, while deniers dispute truth with falsehood.
Moses and Aaron are sent with a sign and a warning to Pharaoh.
God sends a messenger from among the people to call them to worship Him.
Disbelievers mock the messenger selected to guide them.
The demand for signs is answered by defining the messenger as only a clear warner.
Disbelievers refuse the scripture and what preceded it despite its revealed authority.
Records an oath that they would follow guidance if warned, followed by increased aversion when warning comes.
Laments the repeated pattern in which every messenger is mocked.
The book is sent down in truth for people, leaving guidance or misguidance consequential.
Joseph's clear proofs are later doubted again by people previously warned.
The messenger declares the revealed message and calls hearers to go straight to God.
Deniers organize against hearing the Quran so that its guidance will not prevail.
Sets one continuous religious charge delivered to the prophets and made weighty to associators.
Questions whether the reminder should be withheld because its hearers are excessive.
God's signs are recited in truth, challenging what authority could be believed instead.
Describes one who hears God's signs then persists arrogantly as if he never heard them.
The messenger denies novelty and limits himself to following what is revealed.
The jinn recognize the heard book as confirming prior revelation and guiding to truth and a straight path.
Describes people who turn back after guidance has become clear to them.
Jesus announces a later messenger whose arrival is nevertheless called clear magic.
The condemned acknowledge that a warner came and that they denied him.
They recount calling the warner a liar and denying any revelation from God.
Noah reports calling his people by night and day without their response.
His people block their ears and persist arrogantly when called to forgiveness.
